chunks: Al-Kafi: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nadhr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, that he asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Names of Allah and their derivation: From what is 'Allah' derived?

He said: So he said to me: O Hisham, 'Allah' is derived from 'ilah' (god/deity), and 'al-ilah' connotes 'the one who is worshipped'. The name is other than the named. Whoever worships the name without the meaning, he has disbelieved and has not worshipped anything. Whoever worships the name and the meaning, he has disbelieved and worshipped two. Whoever worships the meaning without the name, that is true monotheism. Have you understood, O Hisham?

He said: I said: Increase for me. He said: Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names. If the name were identical to the named, then every one of these names would be a god. But Allah is a meaning to which these names point, and each of them is other than Him. O Hisham, 'bread' is a name for what is eaten, 'water' is a name for what is drunk, 'clothes' is a name for what is worn, 'fire' is a name for what burns. Have you understood, O Hisham, an understanding through which you can repel and defeat our enemies and those who take other deities alongside Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
I said: Yes. He said: May Allah benefit you by it and make you firm, O Hisham. Hisham said: By Allah, no one has defeated me in the subject of Monotheism until I stood in this position.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the name of God and His essence in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith is a cornerstone of Shia theological discourse on divine simplicity, articulated by the dialectical master Hisham ibn al-Hakam to Imam al-Sadiq. It clarifies that 'Allah' is a proper name denoting a unique essence distinct from its attributes, thereby refuting the Mu'tazilite and Ash'arite debates on whether divine names are identical to the divine essence or distinct from it. The Imam’s analogy of bread and water underscores that names are linguistic pointers to realities, ensuring that worship is directed solely at the transcendent meaning rather than the linguistic signifier.
